prize_parts.citation: for a visionary prose of memory, the body and dream, built on an exceptional scale and in an unmistakable voice across a long Romanian-language oeuvre

statement.case_for: Cărtărescu best meets the standard of a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else. On public knowledge, the Orbitor trilogy (Blinding is its first volume) and Solenoid build dense, patterned prose in which memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation form a single project. That project deepens from one major novel to the next instead of repeating itself. The formal ambition is very large, the linguistic density is deliberate, and the work draws on Romanian tradition and on the wider European fantastic and modernist lineage. Attribution is clean: one author, one principal language, and a coherent set of obsessions that supports a single-oeuvre citation, with poetry and essays as context. The career is long and mature, so timing is not an obstacle. I weigh this on the common criteria of distinctiveness, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, imaginative depth and significance across the body of work, not on fame or on how many colleagues also ranked him first.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that the case rests on prose whose force lies in long, intricate Romanian sentences, and I know it through translation and public reception, not the original. The late work may be over-extended or repetitive in places, and I cannot confirm that without a full reading. The poetry and early work are less familiar to me than the major novels, so the citation may in practice rest on a narrower portion of the corpus than the entry suggests. Excess and encyclopedic density may also be weighed differently by colleagues, and that disagreement deserves a serious hearing.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Zurita second, as a highly original poetic project that gives suffering and state violence a memorial form, while noting that the landscape-scale and public interventions are harder to weigh as literature than the printed poems.
responses.response: I share his caution about the extra-textual works, and it is why I keep Zurita below Cărtărescu, at fourth. If the case is built on Purgatorio and Anteparaíso as printed poetry, it is strong and has a clear formal and moral center. If the sky and desert inscriptions carry much of the weight, the will's phrase 'literary works' is under strain. I agree with his point that historical context does not establish merit. Translation loss in long, cumulative, visually structured poems makes me hesitate to place Zurita first. I would keep him as a serious alternative.

responses.point: Sward ranks Adonis second, as a major renewal of Arabic poetic language over many decades, with essays that add intellectual depth. She identifies timing and committee weighing, not depth, as the main question.
responses.response: I agree that depth and duration are not in doubt, and I ranked him lower than she did for a narrower reason. A large part of the achievement lies in Arabic prosody, sound and dialogue with inherited forms, and I cannot assess these directly. I also cannot tell whether the most vital work is concentrated in the earlier decades. I do not think her point about timing should count for or against him on literary grounds. I would want a colleague with firmer access to the Arabic to say how the later poetry compares with the foundational books before moving him above Cărtărescu. I am not dismissing him, and I would welcome that evidence.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson second for an unusually original hybrid form joining scholarship, lyric and visual design. She asks how far the achievement is purely literary, and she ranks Robinson third.
responses.response: Her question about Carson is the right one, and it is not mine to settle. I did not rank Carson in my opening, partly because of the dependence on book-objects and scholarly translation that she names. I agree with her on Robinson. The Gilead novels combine theology, family and American history with real interior depth, and I ranked her third. My reservation is breadth. The fiction is small in volume and the thematic world is narrow, so I do not think it should displace a larger imaginative project, though I would keep her as an alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg notes that Cărtărescu's excess and encyclopedic density could be weighed differently across the committee, and he names the very long, translation-dependent prose as a source of uncertainty.
responses.response: I take that seriously, and it is my own largest reservation. I would not treat density as a flaw in itself, since the excess seems integral to the method. The fair test is whether it stays purposeful across the full length of the major novels or sometimes becomes merely accumulative. I cannot settle that without a full reading, and I would welcome colleagues' specific judgments of individual books. I would resist letting that doubt turn into a preference for a more compact but narrower body of work. On the common criteria, scale combined with a singular voice is a strength.

uncertainties: How much of the Romanian prose's rhythm, syntax and density survives in translation, and whether the translations I know are representative of the whole.
Whether the late large-scale work sustains the originality of the major novels or becomes repetitive.
How the poetry and early prose compare with the major novels. I know them less well, so the citation's scope may be broader than my evidence.
Whether Zurita's non-textual interventions and Adonis's Arabic prosody can be judged adequately by this committee, given limited access to the originals.
I have not independently verified sources or read the texts for this exercise, and my assessments rest on public knowledge and translated reception.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I am a novelist whose published work includes a dream-logic novel, but I treat my own practice as context, not as evidence that I favor any candidate. I have no apparent personal or professional tie to any shortlisted writer.
